name: Noun–adjective gender agreement
rule: A feminine noun (usually ending ة) takes a feminine adjective, which adds ة.

name: Present-tense verb prefixes (he / she / they)
rule: The present-tense verb prefix changes with the subject: يَـ (he), تَـ (she), يَـ…ونَ (they).

name: Sun & moon letters (definite-article assimilation)
rule: ال is pronounced before moon letters; before the 14 sun letters ل is silent and the consonant doubles.

name: Singular, dual & plural nouns
rule: An Arabic noun is singular (بَيْتٌ), dual, or plural. The dual is regular — add ـَانِ to any noun: كِتَابٌ ← كِتَابَانِ (two books). Plurals are either sound — masculine ـُونَ (مُعَلِّمُونَ), feminine ـَاتٌ (طَاوِلَاتٌ) — or broken, an internal reshaping learned with each word: كِتَابٌ ← كُتُبٌ. A plural of non-human things is treated as feminine singular for agreement: كُتُبٌ جَمِيلَةٌ.
commonErrors: Giving a non-human plural a plural adjective: كُتُبٌ كِبَارٌ instead of كُتُبٌ كَبِيرَةٌ.
Expecting one plural ending for every noun — broken plurals vary and are learned individually.

name: Definite & indefinite (ال and tanwīn)
rule: A noun is indefinite or definite. Indefinite nouns end in tanwīn — a doubled final vowel, usually ـٌ ("-un"): كِتَابٌ (a book). Definite nouns take the prefix الـ and lose the tanwīn: الْكِتَابُ (the book). الـ and tanwīn never appear on the same word.
commonErrors: Writing الـ and tanwīn together: الْكِتَابٌ.
Dropping the tanwīn from an indefinite noun — بَاب on its own should be بَابٌ.

name: The nominal sentence (no verb "to be")
rule: A nominal sentence has no verb. It puts a definite topic (mubtadaʾ) next to an indefinite comment (khabar): الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ = "the-house big" = "The house is big." Arabic has no present-tense word for "is" or "are". The khabar agrees with the topic in gender.
commonErrors: Looking for a word that means "is" — there is none.
Making the khabar definite: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ means "the big house", not a sentence.

name: Demonstratives (هَذَا / هَذِهِ / هَؤُلَاءِ)
rule: هَذَا (this, m.), هَذِهِ (this, f.) and هَؤُلَاءِ (these, pl.) point at something and agree with its gender. Before an indefinite noun they form a sentence: هَذَا كِتَابٌ (this is a book). Before a definite noun they mean "this …": هَذَا الْكِتَابُ (this book).
commonErrors: Using هَذَا with a feminine noun: هَذَا بِنْتٌ should be هَذِهِ بِنْتٌ.
Reading هَذَا الْكِتَابُ as a full sentence — with the definite noun it is just "this book".

name: Attached possessive pronouns (ـِي ـكَ ـهُ ـهَا ـنَا ـكُمْ ـهُمْ)
rule: Possession is shown by a suffix on the noun, not a separate word: ـِي (my), ـكَ (your, m.), ـكِ (your, f.), ـهُ (his), ـهَا (her). A noun with a possessive suffix is already definite, so it takes no الـ and no tanwīn: كِتَابِي (my book), بَيْتُهُ (his house). The same mechanic extends to plural antecedents with three more suffixes: ـنَا (our, no gender split — بَيْتُنَا, "our house"), ـكُمْ (your, plural — أَيْنَ كِتَابُكُمْ؟, "where is your book?"), and ـهُمْ (their — مَدْرَسَتُهُمْ, "their school"). ـكُمْ and ـهُمْ are the masculine/mixed-group forms — the same default convention already used for the independent pronoun هُمْ ("they, masculine/mixed group"). Arabic also has specifically-feminine-plural forms (ـكُنَّ "your, f.pl.," ـهُنَّ "their, f.pl.") and dual forms (ـكُمَا "your, dual," ـهُمَا "their, dual") — rare enough at this level to name here and leave for later, the same way dual relative pronouns and Form IX stayed past B1.
commonErrors: Adding الـ to a possessed noun: الْكِتَابِي.
Keeping the tanwīn before the suffix: كِتَابٌي.
Using a singular suffix (ـهُ, ـهَا) for a plural antecedent — a group of people needs ـهُمْ ("their"), not ـهُ repeated for each member.

name: Core prepositions (فِي عَلَى مِنْ إِلَى مَعَ بِـ لِـ)
rule: The common prepositions are فِي (in), عَلَى (on), مِنْ (from), إِلَى (to), مَعَ (with), and the prefixes بِـ (with / by) and لِـ (for / to). The noun after a preposition is in the genitive — with الـ it ends ـِ (فِي الْبَيْتِ), indefinite it ends ـٍ (فِي بَيْتٍ).
commonErrors: Leaving a gap after بِـ or لِـ — they attach directly: بِالْقَلَمِ, not بِ الْقَلَمِ.
Using the ـُ ending after a preposition: فِي الْبَيْتُ should be فِي الْبَيْتِ.

name: Negating the nominal sentence (لَيْسَ / لَا / مَا)
rule: To negate a nominal sentence use لَيْسَ (is / are not) before the comment: لَيْسَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرًا (the house is not big) — the comment takes ـً after لَيْسَ. لَا negates the noun that follows it ("no …", "there is no …"); مَا is a plainer "not" before the comment.
commonErrors: Using لَا where لَيْسَ is needed — لَا الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ is not a sentence.
Forgetting the ـً on the comment after لَيْسَ: لَيْسَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ.

name: Counting nouns: 1-2 vs. 3-10
rule: وَاحِد (one) and اِثْنَان (two) don't count a noun the way English does — the noun itself already shows the number: كِتَابٌ (a book) is already singular, كِتَابَانِ (two books) is already dual (see gr:noun-number) — وَاحِد only gets added for emphasis, agreeing with the noun. From ثَلَاثَة (three) to عَشَرَة (ten), the number is followed by the noun in its plural, genitive form: ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ (three books). The reversed masculine/feminine agreement you can already see on ثَلَاثَةُ (a "feminine-form" number counting a masculine noun) is a real rule, saved for a later, dedicated unit rather than rushed here.
commonErrors: Treating اِثْنَان + noun like 3-10 and reaching for a plural instead of the dual.
Expecting the counted noun after 3-10 to look like an English plural rather than the noun's own (often broken) plural, in the genitive.

name: The verbal sentence & past tense (Form I)
rule: Arabic's other sentence type starts with a verb, not a topic: فِعْل – فَاعِل – مَفْعُول (verb – subject – object) is the neutral word order (VSO) — فَعَلَ الْوَلَدُ ذَلِكَ (the boy did that). A subject-first order is also grammatical and common, especially for emphasis or when the subject opens the sentence as a topic. The past tense of a Form I verb like ذَهَبَ (dhahaba, "he went" — every verb lexeme's own citation form) conjugates by changing its ending: هُوَ ذَهَبَ، هِيَ ذَهَبَتْ، هُمْ ذَهَبُوا، أَنَا ذَهَبْتُ، أَنْتَ ذَهَبْتَ، أَنْتِ ذَهَبْتِ، نَحْنُ ذَهَبْنَا.
commonErrors: Expecting a fixed subject-verb-object order like English — Arabic's default is verb-first, and the verb still agrees with a subject that comes after it.
Reusing the dictionary form (هو ذَهَبَ) for every person instead of changing the ending — the ending alone carries "I", "you", "we", etc.

name: كَانَ — the nominal sentence in the past
rule: كَانَ (kāna, "was / were") moves a nominal sentence into the past. It works like the nominal sentence's own topic-comment pair, except the comment (خَبَر كَانَ) becomes accusative: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ (the house is big) → كَانَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرًا (the house was big) — بَيْتُ stays nominative as كان's own subject (اِسْم كَانَ), and كَبِيرٌ's tanwīn shifts from ـٌ to ـًا. كان's own conjugation is irregular (a hollow root, و, that disappears in some forms): كَانَ (he was), كَانَتْ (she was), كَانُوا (they were), كُنْتُ (I was).
commonErrors: Leaving the comment nominative after كان: كَانَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ should be كَانَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرًا.
Conjugating كان like a regular Form I verb — its middle radical (و) drops out in several forms, so it must be learned as its own irregular pattern.

name: The genitive construct (إِضَافَة / iḍāfa)
rule: Two nouns in sequence express possession — no word for "of" is needed: بَيْتُ الرَّجُلِ (the man's house, literally "house-of the-man"). The first noun (مُضَاف) takes whatever case its role in the sentence needs but drops its own الـ and tanwīn; the second noun (مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ) is always genitive and carries the definiteness for the whole phrase — the first noun is never written with الـ even though the phrase as a whole is definite.
commonErrors: Adding الـ to the first noun: الْبَيْتُ الرَّجُلِ is wrong — only the second noun takes الـ.
Forgetting the genitive on the second noun — بَيْتُ الرَّجُلُ should be بَيْتُ الرَّجُلِ.
Inserting an adjective between the two nouns — a describing word goes after the whole iḍāfa, not inside it.

name: Counting 11-99 and كِتَابًا vs. كُتُبٍ
rule: 11 through 99 share one big difference from 3-10: the counted noun is singular and accusative (تمييز), not plural genitive — عِنْدِي خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا (fifteen books), never a plural. أَحَدَ عَشَرَ (11) and اثْنَا عَشَرَ (12) are irregular compounds, each with its own feminine (إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ، اثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ) — best learned as a pair rather than derived from a rule. From 13 to 19 the pattern is systematic: the ones-digit keeps the reversed agreement already known from 3-10 (ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ), while عَشَر/عَشْرَة agrees normally with the noun's gender instead. 20 through 90 are invariant — the same word counts a masculine or feminine noun alike (عِشْرُونَ) — though they still change for case: عِشْرُونَ (nominative), عِشْرِينَ (accusative/genitive), unlike 11-19 which stay fixed regardless of case. 21-99 compound as ones-digit + وَ + tens (وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ, 21) — the ones-digit behaves exactly as it would alone. مِائَة (100) is different again: it governs a singular GENITIVE noun through iḍāfa, not accusative — مِائَةُ كِتَابٍ.
commonErrors: Using a plural noun after 11-99 the way 3-10 do: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كُتُبٍ is wrong — it should be أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا.
Changing عِشْرُونَ (or any tens word) for gender — it's invariant; only a compound's ones-digit (like the وَاحِدٌ in 21) changes.
Treating مِائَة like 11-99 and giving it an accusative noun — مِائَة takes a genitive noun instead, the same government as 3-10.

name: Telling time (السَّاعَة + the ordinal)
rule: Telling time pairs a definite noun, السَّاعَة (the hour/clock), with a definite ordinal agreeing with it — a complete phrase on its own, the same way English can just answer "two o'clock" with no verb: السَّاعَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ (it's two o'clock). One o'clock is the one exception: it uses the cardinal الْوَاحِدَة (feminine "one"), not an ordinal — there's no "الأُولَى o'clock". Two through ten use the plain ordinal (الثَّانِيَة، الثَّالِثَة، الرَّابِعَة…); eleven and twelve compound an ordinal ones-word with the teen-marker exactly the way cardinal numbers do (الْحَادِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ، الثَّانِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ) — and stay fixed on ـَ regardless of case, the same indeclinable pattern the cardinal teens already showed. Minutes attach with وَ for "past" (السَّاعَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ, half past two) or إِلَّا for "to" (السَّاعَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا, quarter to four).
commonErrors: Using the cardinal (اثنان) instead of the ordinal (الثَّانِيَة) for two o'clock and beyond.
Reaching for الأُولَى (the ordinal "first") for one o'clock — it's the one hour that keeps the cardinal, الْوَاحِدَة.
Using وَ where إِلَّا is needed — quarter TO the hour is إِلَّا, not وَ: السَّاعَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا, not وَرُبْع.

name: Dates (the ordinal + مِنْ + the month)
rule: A date pairs a definite ordinal with the month via مِنْ: الثَّالِثُ مِنْ سِبْتَمْبِر (the third of September) — a complete phrase on its own, the same elliptical pattern already used for telling time. Because يَوْم (day) is masculine, unlike السَّاعَة, dates use the masculine ordinals — the exact same roots already known from telling time's feminine set (ثَانِي، ثَالِث، رَابِع…), just without the ة. أَوَّل (1st) is irregular, its own word rather than built on that shared pattern. ثَانِي (2nd) is a defective noun (نَاقِص): its true indefinite form drops the ي with tanwīn (ثَانٍ), while the definite form used in dates keeps it (الثَّانِي). Month names are transliterated loanwords and, like other such proper nouns, are treated here without extra case marking of their own. To turn the bare date-phrase into a full sentence, add هُوَ, referring back to الْيَوْمَ (today, accusative — the normal case for a time adverbial): الْيَوْمَ هُوَ الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَارِس (today is the fifth of March).
commonErrors: Using a cardinal instead of an ordinal for the day: خَمْسَة مِنْ مَارِس instead of الْخَامِسُ مِنْ مَارِس.
Reaching for the feminine ordinal used for telling time instead of the masculine — يَوْم is masculine, unlike السَّاعَة.
Treating أَوَّل like the other ordinals — it doesn't follow the فَاعِل pattern the rest share.

name: Root & pattern (الجَذْر وَالوَزْن)
rule: Most Arabic words are built from a root (جَذْر) — usually three consonants carrying a core, abstract meaning — poured into a pattern (وَزْن) that adds a grammatical role: a place, an instrument, an action, a doer. كَتَبَ (he wrote), كِتَاب (book), and مَكْتَبَة (library) all share the root ك-ت-ب ("write"); the vowels and extra letters around those three consonants belong to the pattern, not the root. A bare root isn't itself a pronounceable word — د-ر-س only becomes sayable once a pattern is applied: دَرْس (lesson), مَدْرَسَة (school, literally "the place where studying happens"). Recognising a shared root is a shortcut to guessing an unfamiliar word's rough meaning long before you know the whole vocabulary.
commonErrors: Assuming any two words that merely look alike share a root — root-sharing means the same three consonants in the same order, not surface resemblance.

Expecting one pattern to always carry one fixed meaning — patterns are strong tendencies (مَفْعَل often marks "place of," مِفْعَال often marks "instrument"), not absolute rules; the same pattern surfaces different senses on different roots.

Treating the root like an English base word that gets prefixes/suffixes stuck on it — the root is an abstract three-consonant skeleton that never stands alone as a word; it gets its vowels and shape entirely from the pattern poured into it.

name: Derived verb forms (الأَوْزَان)
rule: A root can be poured into more than one verb pattern, not just Form I's bare فَعَلَ — nine more patterns (Forms II–X) build related but distinct verbs from the same three consonants: II فَعَّلَ (doubled middle letter), III فَاعَلَ (a long ا after the first letter), IV أَفْعَلَ (أَ prefixed), V تَفَعَّلَ (تَ + Form II's pattern), VI تَفَاعَلَ (تَ + Form III's pattern), VII اِنْفَعَلَ (اِنْ prefixed), VIII اِفْتَعَلَ (a ت infixed after the first letter), IX اِفْعَلَّ (doubled final letter, colors and physical defects), X اِسْتَفْعَلَ (اِسْتَ prefixed). Seven of these appear in verbs you already knew before this lesson: جَرَّبَ (II, "to try"), سَافَرَ (III, "to travel"), أَرَادَ and أَغْلَقَ (IV, "to want" and "to close"), تَكَلَّمَ (V, "to speak"), اِشْتَرَى (VIII, "to buy"), اِسْتَيْقَظَ (X, "to wake up") — same discipline as gr:root-pattern, applied to verbs instead of nouns. Forms VI and VII each needed one genuinely new word: تَكَاتَبَ (VI, "to correspond," built on the same root ك-ت-ب as كَتَبَ/كِتَاب/مَكْتَبَة), and اِنْفَتَحَ/اِنْغَلَقَ (VII, "to open/close by itself") taught as minimal pairs with the already-known فَتَحَ/أَغْلَقَ ("to open/close [something]"). The forms carry real tendencies: II often causative/intensive ("to make X happen" or "to X thoroughly"), III often reciprocal or effort directed at someone, IV often causative (similar to II, but often built from a plain noun or adjective rather than another verb), V the reflexive of II ("to become X'd," or to do II's action to yourself), VI the reciprocal of III ("to do X to/with each other"), VII the passive/reflexive of Form I ("for something to become X'd" — it never takes a human agent as its subject, which is exactly why اِنْفَتَحَ/اِنْغَلَقَ pair so naturally with "the door opened/closed" rather than "someone opened/closed it"), VIII a reflexive/middle-voice sense ("to do X for yourself"), X "to seek/consider X" or a reflexive-causative sense ("to render yourself X").
commonErrors: Expecting a fixed meaning for every form on every root — like noun patterns in gr:root-pattern, these are strong tendencies, not rules a dictionary enforces: اِشْتَرَى doesn't transparently mean "to seek to sell" from ش-ر-ي's buy/sell sense, it's simply lexicalized as "to buy."

Assuming a derived form's Form I counterpart always exists as an actual word — تَكَلَّمَ (V) has no attested Form II كَلَّمَ used the same way in everyday MSA; the *pattern's* meaning tendency still holds even when the "paired" form isn't itself a common word.

Confusing the doubled middle letter of Form II (فَعَّلَ, e.g. جَرَّبَ) with the long ا after the first letter of Form III (فَاعَلَ, e.g. سَافَرَ) — they look similar in translit but are written and pronounced differently.

Giving a Form VII verb a human subject — اِنْفَتَحَ الْبَابُ ("the door opened") is natural, but a person doesn't اِنْفَتَحَ; Form VII describes something undergoing an action, not someone performing one.

name: Relative clauses (الَّذِي / الَّتِي)
rule: الَّذِي (masculine) and الَّتِي (feminine) mean "who / which / that" and introduce a relative clause — but only after a DEFINITE antecedent. الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي سَافَرَ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ ("the man who traveled to the city") is definite (الرَّجُلُ carries الـ), so الَّذِي is required. Drop the antecedent's الـ and الَّذِي disappears too: رَجُلٌ سَافَرَ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ ("a man [who] traveled to the city") — Arabic doesn't mark an indefinite relative clause with any pronoun at all; the clause just follows the noun directly. الَّذِي/الَّتِي agree with the antecedent's gender, never the clause's own internal grammar — الَّتِي is chosen because الْمَرْأَةُ (the woman) is feminine, whatever gender the verb after it happens to be. The clause that follows — جملة الصلة — has no case role of its own; that's a fuller idea only formally parsed much later (C1), mentioned here just so the term isn't left unexplained. SUBJECT-relative clauses need nothing extra: الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي سَافَرَ..., "the man who [he] traveled..." — the verb's built-in subject already is the antecedent. OBJECT-relative clauses, where the antecedent is the clause's OBJECT instead, need an extra resumptive pronoun suffix on the clause's verb, pointing back at the antecedent — the same attached-pronoun suffixes gr:attached-possessive and إنّ's family (gr:inna-sisters) already use: الْكِتَابُ الَّذِي قَرَأْتُهُ جَمِيلٌ ("the book that I read is beautiful") — قَرَأْتُ alone would mean "I read [something unspecified]"; the ـهُ on the end makes it "I read it," resuming الْكِتَابُ. الْمَرْأَةُ الَّتِي رَأَيْتُهَا سَعِيدَةٌ ("the woman that I saw is happy") does the same with ـهَا. Both الَّذِي and الَّتِي are strictly singular — a PLURAL, human antecedent needs its own pronoun: الَّذِينَ (masculine plural) and اللَّاتِي (feminine plural). Both apply gr:noun-number's already-taught sound-plural patterns to already-known singulars: الْمُعَلِّمُونَ الَّذِينَ فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ مَشْغُولُونَ ("the teachers who are at school are busy," مُعَلِّم → مُعَلِّمُونَ) and الْمُعَلِّمَاتُ اللَّاتِي فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ مَشْغُولَاتٌ ("the [female] teachers who are at school are busy," مُعَلِّمَة → مُعَلِّمَاتٌ). A non-human plural still takes singular-feminine الَّتِي, unchanged from gr:noun-number's own rule — الَّذِينَ/اللَّاتِي are for PEOPLE specifically. Arabic also has DUAL relative pronouns (اللَّذَانِ/اللَّذَيْنِ and feminine counterparts, themselves case-inflected) — rare enough at this level to name here and leave for later, the same way Form IX stayed past B1.
commonErrors: Using الَّذِي/الَّتِي after an indefinite antecedent — رَجُلٌ الَّذِي سَافَرَ is wrong; drop الَّذِي entirely once the antecedent loses its الـ.
Matching الَّذِي/الَّتِي to the wrong gender — they agree with the antecedent noun (الرَّجُلُ → الَّذِي, الْمَرْأَةُ → الَّتِي), not with anything inside the clause that follows.
Forgetting the resumptive pronoun on an object-relative clause — الْكِتَابُ الَّذِي قَرَأْتُ جَمِيلٌ is incomplete; the verb needs قَرَأْتُهُ, with ـهُ pointing back at الْكِتَابُ.
Using singular الَّذِي/الَّتِي with a plural, human antecedent — a group of teachers needs الَّذِينَ/اللَّاتِي, not الَّذِي/الَّتِي repeated for each one.

name: إنّ وأخواتها (Inna and Its Sisters)
rule: إنّ وأخواتها ("inna and its sisters") is a family of particles that enters a nominal sentence and shifts one side's case — the mirror image of كَانَ (gr:kana). Where كَانَ leaves the subject nominative and pushes the predicate to accusative, إنّ's family does the reverse: it pushes the subject (اِسْم إِنَّ) to accusative and leaves the predicate (خَبَر إِنَّ) nominative. الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ ("the house is big") → إِنَّ الْبَيْتَ كَبِيرٌ ("indeed the house is big") — الْبَيْتُ's ـُ becomes ـَ; كَبِيرٌ stays exactly as it was. إِنَّ opens a sentence for emphasis ("indeed / truly") and is the family's namesake and most frequent member. أَنَّ subordinates a nominal clause as "that" after a verb of saying, hearing, or knowing: سَمِعْتُ أَنَّ الطَّقْسَ جَمِيلٌ الْيَوْمَ ("I heard that the weather is beautiful today") — أَنَّ's own subject-clause still obeys the same accusative-subject rule. أَنَّ is not to be confused with أَنْ, the unrelated subjunctive "to" that subordinates a following verb instead of a nominal clause — a separate B1 topic. لِأَنَّ ("because"), already known since A1, is transparently لِ + أَنَّ and governs the same accusative-subject rule: هِيَ سَعِيدَةٌ لِأَنَّ الطَّقْسَ دَافِئٌ ("she is happy because the weather is warm"). كَأَنَّ ("as if") makes a comparison: كَأَنَّ الطَّقْسَ بَارِدٌ الْيَوْمَ ("it's as if the weather is cold today"). لٰكِنَّ is the HEAVY "but" — a real sister of إنّ, shifting the following noun to accusative: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ لٰكِنَّ الْحَدِيقَةَ صَغِيرَةٌ ("the house is big, but the garden is small"); it is a distinct word from the already-known LIGHT لَكِنْ, which does not shift case at all. لَعَلَّ ("perhaps") expresses hope or expectation: لَعَلَّ الطَّقْسَ جَمِيلٌ غَدًا ("perhaps the weather will be beautiful tomorrow"). لَيْتَ ("would that / I wish") expresses an irrealis wish, usually for something unlikely or unattainable, not an ordinary polite request: لَيْتَ الطَّقْسَ دَافِئٌ ("would that the weather were warm"). That completes all ten traditionally-listed sisters by name, seven of them (إِنَّ, أَنَّ, لِأَنَّ, كَأَنَّ, لٰكِنَّ, لَعَلَّ, لَيْتَ) with a full worked example here. Instead of a following noun, any sister of إنّ can take an attached pronoun suffix directly as its subject — the exact same possessive suffixes already taught in gr:attached-possessive (ـهُ his/him/it, ـهَا her/it, ـكَ your m., ـكِ your f.), just attaching to the particle itself instead of to a noun: إِنَّهُ سَعِيدٌ ("indeed he is happy") attaches ـهُ straight onto إِنَّ, playing the same role a following noun's accusative form would; سَمِعْتُ أَنَّهَا سَعِيدَةٌ ("I heard that she is happy") attaches ـهَا to أَنَّ; هُوَ سَعِيدٌ لِأَنَّهُ فِي الْبَيْتِ ("he is happy because he is at home") shows the same mechanic on لِأَنَّ. The 1st-person suffix is irregular after إنّ's family — إِنَّ + ي surfaces as إِنِّي, not the "expected" إِنَّنِي — flagged here as a heads-up, not taught as its own rule yet.
commonErrors: Leaving the subject after any sister of إنّ in the nominative — إِنَّ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ is wrong; the noun right after any of the ten sisters must take the accusative ending, exactly the reverse of what a learner's كَانَ instinct expects.
Confusing أَنَّ ("that," subordinates a nominal clause) with أَنْ (the subjunctive "to," subordinates a following verb) — the two are unrelated words that transliterate almost identically.
Confusing لِأَنَّ/لٰكِنَّ (heavy, case-marking "because"/"but") with لَكِنْ (light "but," no shadda, does not shift case) — different words, different jobs, only superficially similar in shape.
Treating إنّ's case-shift as optional or stylistic — like كَانَ, it is a grammatical requirement of the particle, not emphasis added on top of an unchanged sentence.

Treating لَيْتَ's wish as an ordinary request or hope — لَيْتَ specifically marks something unlikely or impossible (an irrealis wish), which is why it reads differently from لَعَلَّ's more realistic "perhaps."
Expecting a following noun after every sister of إنّ and treating the attached pronoun as optional — when no noun is stated, the pronoun suffix IS the subject, not something left out.

name: The full case system (الإِعْرَاب) — رَفْع / نَصْب / جَرّ
rule: Arabic marks a noun's grammatical role with one of three cases, each with its own ending on a regular (triptote) noun. رَفْع (raf', nominative) — ḍamma ـُ, or tanwīn ḍamma ـٌ if indefinite — marks a مُبْتَدَأ, a خَبَر, or a فَاعِل: الْأَبُ سَعِيدٌ ("the father is happy") — both الْأَبُ and سَعِيدٌ are رَفْع. نَصْب (naṣb, accusative) — fatḥa ـَ, or tanwīn fatḥa ـً — marks a مَفْعُول بِهِ: قَرَأْتُ الْكِتَابَ ("I read the book") — الْكِتَابَ is نَصْب. جَرّ (jarr, genitive) — kasra ـِ, or tanwīn kasra ـٍ — marks a مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ, or any noun after a preposition: بَابُ الْبَيْتِ ("the door of the house") — الْبَيْتِ is جَرّ. None of this is new: you've been producing these three endings correctly since A2 without naming the system behind them — gr:idafa's second term is always جَرّ, gr:kana's predicate is always نَصْب, and every sister of gr:inna-sisters pushes its subject to نَصْب. إِعْرَاب is simply the name for reading (or producing) the case ending that a word's role already requires. This part covers only REGULAR nouns — ones that take the full ḍamma/fatḥa/kasra + tanwīn system. Two irregular layers mark case differently. الْأَسْمَاء الْخَمْسَة ("the five nouns") — أَب (father), أَخ (brother), حَم (father-in-law), فَم (mouth), ذُو (possessor of) — swap the short vowel for a long one when they are the first term of an iḍāfa (not when a pronoun like ـِي attaches directly): وَ for رَفْع, ا for نَصْب, ي for جَرّ. أَخُو الطَّالِبِ مُعَلِّمٌ ("the student's brother is a teacher") — أَخُو is رَفْع, marked by وَ, not the ضمة a regular noun would take; رَأَيْتُ أَبَا الطَّالِبِ ("I saw the student's father") — أَبَا is نَصْب, marked by ا; كِتَابُ أَخِي الطَّالِبِ جَدِيدٌ ("the student's brother's book is new") — أَخِي is جَرّ, marked by ي. حَم، فَم، ذُو follow the same pattern but are rare outside classical or very formal registers. The sound plurals also swap a short vowel for a longer marker, but only in نَصْب/جَرّ. The sound masculine plural (ـُونَ in رَفْع) takes ـِينَ for BOTH نَصْب and جَرّ: رَأَيْتُ الْمُعَلِّمِينَ ("I saw the teachers") — الْمُعَلِّمِينَ is نَصْب, not the ـُونَ you might expect. The sound feminine plural (ـَاتٌ in رَفْع) is regular except in نَصْب, where it unexpectedly takes the same kasra-tanwīn ending (ـَاتٍ) as its own جَرّ form, instead of the fatḥa a regular noun would take: رَأَيْتُ الْمُعَلِّمَاتِ ("I saw the [female] teachers") — الْمُعَلِّمَاتِ is نَصْب here, spelled exactly like جَرّ. The last irregular layer: diptotes (مَمْنُوع مِنَ الصَّرْف) — a closed set of noun shapes (certain broken-plural patterns like مَفَاعِل/أَفْعِلَاء, and every proper name of a person) that drop tanwin entirely and, when INDEFINITE, take fatha instead of kasra for جَرّ: هَذِهِ مَكَاتِبُ جَدِيدَةٌ ("these are new offices") is رَفْع; رَأَيْتُ مَكَاتِبَ جَدِيدَةً ("I saw new offices") is نَصْب; هَذَا بَيْتُ أَصْدِقَاءَ ("this is a friends' house") is جَرّ, marked by fatha, not kasra. That irregularity disappears the moment the noun becomes DEFINITE — by الـ, or by being the second term of an iḍāfa whose own definiteness carries through: هَذَا بَيْتُ الْأَصْدِقَاءِ ("this is the friends' house") takes the regular kasra, because الـ on الْأَصْدِقَاءِ makes it definite again. Diptotes, the five nouns, and the sound plurals are now all named and taught. Case marking on the VERB itself (رفع/نصب/جزم of the present tense) remains a wholly separate system, still not covered here.
commonErrors: Treating إِعْرَاب as new grammar rather than a new name for endings already being produced correctly — every case ending in this lesson's examples was already required by a rule taught back at A2/B1 (gr:idafa, gr:kana, gr:inna-sisters).

Assuming every noun uses ḍamma/fatḥa/kasra — diptotes and the five nouns/sound plurals mark case differently; the first look at this grammar point deliberately stayed inside the regular system before naming the irregular layer.
Expecting the five nouns or the sound masculine plural to take a short-vowel ending like a regular noun — both categories mark case with a long vowel (و/ا/ي, or ـُونَ/ـِينَ) instead.
Assuming the sound feminine plural is fully regular — its نَصْب form unexpectedly matches its own جَرّ form (kasra), not the fatḥa a regular noun would take.
Confusing a word's case (رفع/نصب/جر, a property of nouns) with a verb's mood (رفع/نصب/جزم of the present tense) — same three Arabic names, different system, not covered by this grammar point.

Assuming a diptote always takes fatha for جَرّ — the irregularity only applies when the noun is INDEFINITE. Once definite (by الـ or by iḍāfa to a definite noun), it declines completely regularly, kasra included.

name: Present-tense mood (الْفِعْل الْمُضَارِع) — مَرْفُوع / مَنْصُوب / مَجْزُوم
rule: The present tense has three moods, marked on the verb's own ending — using the same three Arabic names as noun case (gr:case-system), but a completely separate system: this marks the VERB, not a noun's role. مَرْفُوع (the default) is the plain present tense already known since A1: ḍamma ـُ — هُوَ يَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ ("he goes to school"). مَنْصُوب replaces that ḍamma with fatḥa ـَ, triggered by a particle right before the verb — أَنْ ("to," after a verb like أَرَادَ) and لَنْ ("will never"): هُوَ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَذْهَبَ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ ("he wants to go to school"); هُوَ لَنْ يَذْهَبَ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ ("he will never go to school"). مَجْزُوم drops that vowel entirely — sukūn, no ending vowel at all — triggered here by لَمْ, which negates the PAST using a present-tense verb: هُوَ لَمْ يَذْهَبْ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ ("he did not go to school") — the only way taught so far to negate a verbal past-tense sentence; gr:negation-a1's لَيْسَ/لَا/مَا only negate a NOMINAL sentence. Other subjunctive particles (كَيْ, حَتَّى, لِـ) and other jussive triggers (لَا النَّاهِيَة the prohibition, لَام الْأَمْر the command particle, and the conditional particles إِنْ/مَنْ/مَا) are named here, not taught yet. Plural and dual forms mark مَجْزُوم differently — by dropping the final ن instead of adding a sukūn (تَذْهَبُونَ → لَمْ تَذْهَبُوا) — deferred to a later unit.
commonErrors: Confusing a verb's mood (رفع/نصب/جزم, marked on the verb itself) with a noun's case (رفع/نصب/جر, marked on a noun's role) — the same three Arabic names for two of them, but an entirely different system. gr:case-system's own rule text flags this same confusion from the other direction.
Assuming لَمْ + a present-tense verb describes something happening now — لَمْ negates the PAST, even though the verb after it keeps its present-tense shape.
Using مَنْصُوب or مَجْزُوم without one of their trigger particles directly before the verb — with nothing before it, or after a different particle, the verb stays مَرْفُوع.
